newsitem.title: UK: European bonds seen converging at higher yields.
newsitem.headline: European bonds seen converging at higher yields.

text.p: European bond prices are shold fall ahead of an expected broader-based entry for European economic and monetary union (EMU), which means their yields will converge at higher levels, analysts said on Friday.

Nations expected to participate in EMU are supposed to meet certain economic criteria for entry. Because of that, those countries' interest rates should, theoretically, converge, or move toward a common level, since the level of risk in those countries should be roughly the same.
But weaker EMU entry criteria would depress debt prices because it would allow a greater number of nations with potentially higher levels of debt to participate.
Governments with high debt levels are forced to borrow more heavily in bond markets, increasing supply and so reducing bond prices. Bond prices move inversely with yields.

"We have convergence at lower yield levels now. But yields in core Europe will rise, and we will converge at higher levels," said Graham McDevitt, head of bond strategy at Paribas Capital Markets in London.

A broader, more inclusive EMU was looking more likely on Friday after French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said late on Thursday France would fail to meet one of the key Maastricht criteria for EMU.
Strauss-Kahn said for the first time France would definitely not be able to pare its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year.
On Friday, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl dismissed talk of softening criteria or delaying EMU.
He said the planned single euro currency would be introduced fully in line with the Maastricht criteria and that any talk of a delay could mean the project might be indefinitely postponed.
European bonds held steady after the remarks.
"Two of the main players have reiterated their position," said David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International Europe. "They have said nothing new."
But prospects have risen for a wider range of nations participating in the euro, analysts said.
"It is making people more aware of the weak euro scenario," said McDevitt.

Bunds have gained this week against U.S. Treasuries, with the 10-year yield spread widening to 92 basis points from 75 basis points. But the widening reflects short-term switching from Treasuries, rather than sustainable gains for Bunds, McDevitt said.
Italian bonds will benefit from renewed hopes of single currency entry, analysts said.
"Italy will benefit from a greater flexibility towards the (Maastricht) treaty, though there are still question marks over whether it will make it into EMU first time around," said Brickman.

Italian government bonds hit a record low yield spread of 111 basis points against Bunds on Wednesday. The 10-year spread can narrow to 100 basis points on a three-month basis, Brickman said. It was quoted at 119 basis points at 1400 GMT.

Bond convergence between Italy and Germany would only suffer if the latest round of comments was seen as increasing the likelihood of an EMU delay, said Jean-Francois Mercier, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.
"But that risk looks moderate because of the French government's commitment to the start date. It scaled back its demands quite a bit to sign the stability pact in Amsterdam."

France's new socialist government agreed on a stability pact to keep budget deficits in check post-EMU in return for a resolution on jobs and growth at a summit of European Union leaders in Amsterdam earlier this month.
